chunks: "Differential signalling gets used wherever noise, ground offsets, speed, or EMI are a problem, which is most of the interesting interfaces. There are a few categories.
First, long cables and noisy environments: RS-485, CAN, and Ethernet on twisted pair.
The nodes can have different ground potentials and the cable picks up interference, so you need the common-mode rejection.
Second, high-speed digital links: USB, PCIe, SATA, HDMI and DisplayPort, LVDS displays and camera interfaces.
At those rates single-ended swings would cause too much EMI and be too sensitive to noise, so they use small differential swings and controlled impedance pairs.

Third, low-level analog signals: microphones, which use balanced XLR cables, and sensors like bridges and thermocouples, which use differential amplifier inputs, because the signal is millivolts and the noise is much bigger, but common-mode.
And fourth, precision conversion: differential ADC inputs and clock distribution, where you want the extra 6 decibels, lower even-order distortion and rejection of supply noise.
I wouldn't use it for short, slow, on-board lines like a GPIO or an I2C bus. The extra pins and routing aren't worth it there."
